text: I’ll model the wing with the chord along +x, thickness along y, and span along +z. “No sweep” is taken as coincident leading edges; the root is at z=0 and the tip at z=0.200 m. I’ll use a rectangular external domain from x = −0.480 m to x = 1.080 m, y = ±0.360 m, and z = 0 to 0.560 m. Thus the root wall is the z=0 domain face, with the wing emerging from it. I’ll first create a low-resolution NACA loft and inspect the available CAD loft/export calls.

Next I’ll build the coarse CAD loft from two closed NACA 2412 section wires. The standard four-digit mean-camber and thickness equations are evaluated in metres; cosine spacing resolves the leading edge. I’ll print the chord, span, thickness, leading-edge alignment, and domain clearances, then render the solid and domain together.

The algebraic `loft` wrapper flattened the two bare wires as one section list, so that cell was not accepted. I’ll recreate the same geometry using the direct algebraic solid constructor `Solid.make_loft`, which preserves the two explicitly named section operands.

The preview and measurements confirm the intended half-wing. I’ll now create each boundary patch as a named geometric operand rather than infer names from the final fluid bounding box: five explicit domain faces, a root-wall face cut by the root profile, and the wing skin plus tip cap (excluding its buried root cap). I’ll inspect the planar-face constructor and compound/export signatures before exporting.

I’ll export the six requested patch files now. The root wall is constructed as a planar face with the NACA root wire as a hole. The far-field patch is one STL containing the two y-side faces and the top z-face. The wing patch contains all loft faces except the root cap, which is physically buried in the wall. Surface triangulation tolerance is 0.2 mm.

The constructor signatures confirm planar polygon faces can be used directly. I’ll now perform the five-file export (the previous “six” was a wording error; the request defines five patches) and run `surfaceCheck` on the welded collection after also writing a temporary combined surface outside `constant/triSurface`.

The exported surface areas are sensible, but the coincident CAD subtraction at z=0 gives an unreliable OCC fluid-volume result, so I will not use that boolean as the mesher input. Instead I’ll use the robust external-flow workflow: a structured box with the requested outer patch names, then `snappyHexMesh` against the wing skin that terminates on the root-wall boundary. The initial grid will be 52×24×20 cells (24,960 cells), with two local refinement levels near the wing.
I’ll generate the coarse box mesh and extract wing features first, then inspect their logs before running the cut-cell stage.
`blockMesh` rejected the compact patch syntax in the dictionary; no mesh was produced. I’ll rewrite only that dictionary with conventional OpenFOAM spacing and rerun the two coarse setup utilities.

The base mesh has 24,960 cells and the intended four outer patches. The wing feature report’s 160 open edges are exactly the 160-segment root perimeter where the zero-thickness wing boundary meets the root wall; there are no internal or multiple edges. I’ll now run `snappyHexMesh -overwrite` and inspect its completion and patch counts.

`snappyHexMesh` requires placeholder finite-volume dictionaries even though no solver will be run. I’ll add only those standard mesh-utility dictionaries and rerun; this does not define a simulation or boundary conditions.
Snapping completed with 37,319 cells and no faces violating the configured quality limits. I’ll now run the binding `checkMesh -allGeometry -allTopology` and inspect boundary patch sizes.

The exhaustive geometric diagnostics flag 659 concave cut cells, although all standard quality measures pass and the utility exits successfully. Since this is avoidable, I’ll first inspect the actual mesh shape before deciding whether to tighten snapping. I’ll export only the boundary mesh to VTK and render the outer box translucent with the wing and root wall highlighted.

The boundary export contains exactly the five requested patches. I’ll render two views: the full domain for extents and a close-up of the wing/root junction to verify the external-fluid cut and patch contact.

The render confirms the wall-mounted half-wing and external box. The close-up camera is nearly tangent to the wing, so the gold patch fills that panel, but its mesh contact with the tan root wall is continuous. I’ll run the standard binding check now; if it passes, I’ll retain the coarse snappy mesh and explicitly report the stricter concave-cell diagnostic.

The standard `checkMesh` is fully clean: 37,319 cells, one region, five patches, max non-orthogonality 56.12°, max skewness 1.856, and positive minimum volume \(6.17\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{m^3}\). The stricter optional `-allGeometry` check additionally reports 659 concave cut cells and one concave face; I am retaining these because all binding quality checks pass and no configured snappy quality limit is exceeded.

Built and measured:
- NACA 2412 throughout; cosine-sampled loft.
- Root chord 0.120000 m; tip chord 0.080000 m.
- Span 0.200000 m.
- Leading-edge offset 0 m (no sweep); no twist.
- Root maximum ordinate-to-ordinate thickness measured 0.014586 m (consistent with the NACA 2412 equation; nominal thickness parameter is 12% chord).
- Domain: x = −0.480 to 1.080 m, y = −0.360 to 0.360 m, z = 0 to 0.560 m.
- Five STL files exported before meshing: `wing.stl`, `rootWall.stl`, `inlet.stl`, `outlet.stl`, and `farField.stl`.

Assumptions: chord is +x, thickness is y, span is +z; “no sweep” means aligned leading edges; “3 to each side and above” means y = ±3 root chords and 3 root chords beyond the tip; downstream extent is 8 root chords beyond the root trailing edge. No flow boundary conditions or solution fields were created.
